content: Health care needs related to maturation, female hygiene (including menstrual hygiene), and male hygiene are critical areas of focus for adolescents. To address these needs effectively, adolescent-friendly health services, including sexual and reproductive health services (SHS), are designed to be accessible, acceptable, and appropriate for this age group. Schools have a unique potential to deliver comprehensive, long-term, and large-scale health programs to children and adolescents. Globally, the majority of children and adolescents are enrolled in schools, with increasing numbers transitioning from primary to secondary education. The global adjusted net enrollment rates for primary and secondary schools are 89% and 66%, respectively. As such, school health services (SHS) may represent the only institutional mechanism to meet the health needs of most school-aged children and adolescents on a near-daily basis. Operating within an educational setting, SHS are well-positioned to leverage the intrinsic link between health and education. These services function within the broader framework of school health, as articulated by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 1995 with the launch of the Global School Health Initiative. This initiative aimed to improve the health of children, adolescents, and communities through multifaceted health programming in schools. In 2000, the initiative expanded through the Focusing Resources on Effective School Health (FRESH) partnership, which supported countries in developing school health programs and increasing the number of health-promoting schools (HPS). HPS are defined as schools that continuously strengthen their capacity to serve as healthy environments for living, learning, and working. Effectively addressing the health needs of children and adolescents in HPS requires evidence-based interventions that target both health and well-being directly, as well as the structural and social determinants of health. HPS initiatives have demonstrated success in improving health-related behaviors, such as increasing physical activity, fitness, and fruit and vegetable intake, while preventing tobacco use and bullying. School-based interventions, including deworming, insecticide-treated bed net promotion, vaccinations (e.g., tetanus toxoid and HPV), oral health promotion, vision screening with provision of spectacles, micronutrient supplementation, and school feeding programs, have shown excellent cost-effectiveness and high benefit-cost ratios. Investments in adolescent health and education yield significant economic and social returns, ranging from sixto twelve-fold. Expanding access to comprehensive SHS is one of the eight global standards for HPS. However, achieving high coverage, quality, equity, and sustainability of HPS has been challenging in many countries, primarily due to poor integration of health and health promotion into education systems. Recognizing this gap, the 2017 Global Accelerated Action for the Health of Adolescents (AA-HA.) Guidance emphasized the prioritization of school health programs as a step toward universal health coverage (UHC), advocating for every school to become a health-promoting school. In 2018, WHO and UNESCO launched the Making Every School a Health-Promoting School initiative, in collaboration with other United Nations entities such as UNICEF and UNFPA. This initiative developed global standards and implementation guidance for HPS, emphasizing the critical role of SHS. The eight global standards for HPS include government policies and resources, school policies and resources, governance and leadership, community partnerships, curriculum, social-emotional environment, physical environment, and health services. Despite the recognition of their importance, SHS programs in many countries are underfunded, poorly implemented, and lack evidence-based approaches. Challenges include staff shortages, high workloads, insufficient training, and inadequate coordination between health and education sectors. Furthermore, mental health services and injury prevention interventions are often overlooked in routine SHS provision. National SHS frameworks sometimes marginalize or omit the SHS component, even when emphasizing a whole-school approach to health. The WHO guideline on SHS aims to provide national governments and stakeholders with detailed guidance on the effectiveness, acceptability, and content of SHS involving health workers. It supports the development of evidence-informed SHS programs to better meet the health and developmental needs of school-aged children and adolescents. The guideline focuses on services provided by health workers to students in primary or secondary education, either within school premises or through external health services linked to schools. The guideline emphasizes the importance of comprehensive SHS, which include interventions across at least four of seven defined health areas: positive health and development, unintentional injury, violence, sexual and reproductive health (including HIV), communicable diseases, noncommunicable diseases (including oral health, nutrition, and physical activity), and mental health (including substance use and self-harm). It also outlines seven types of SHS activities: health promotion, health education, screening, preventive interventions, clinical assessment, health services management, and care coordination. The development of the guideline followed WHO's standard procedures, including systematic reviews and evidence synthesis. It provides a single overarching recommendation on the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive SHS, along with a menu of potential interventions for implementation. These interventions were assessed and categorized based on expert surveys and global evidence but are not formal WHO guideline recommendations. The guideline is intended for government policymakers, program managers, and stakeholders in the health and education sectors responsible for the well-being of students aged 5–19. Secondary audiences include academics, school health workers, school staff, and students. It aims to contribute to achieving specific Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as ending epidemics of communicable diseases, reducing premature mortality from noncommunicable diseases, promoting mental health, and ensuring universal access to sexual and reproductive health services.
